DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study (Thornbury District Council)

The pilot design is good. It tested the real service, measured results weekly, and reported them by housing type. The cost table also adds up. However, the study contradicts its own pilot data on flats, uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot results, and ignores a treatment capacity limit it states itself. With those corrected, the claim that the service is "fully funded" no longer holds.

## 1. Participation did not hold up in flats

Section 2 says participation was "broadly similar across housing types." Table 1 shows houses at **66%** and flats at **21%**, roughly a third of the house rate. Flats also produced less food waste per participating household: 1.4 kg a week against 1.9 kg.

This is the study's most important finding, and the text reverses it. Low participation in flats is a common problem, usually caused by a lack of outdoor space and by communal bin stores. It normally needs a different approach, such as communal food bins, extra liners or targeted communications. That approach costs money and should be in the plan. With about 10,400 flats in the district, this affects around a fifth of households.

## 2. The 64% participation rate doesn't come from the pilot

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." The pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and 64% appears nowhere in Table 1. The district has the same share of flats as the pilot (20%), so 57% is the directly comparable figure.

| Basis | Annual tonnage |
|---|---|
| As stated: 52,000 × 64% × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks | ~3,290 t |
| Pilot's overall rate: 52,000 × 57% × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks | ~2,930 t |
| **By housing type:** houses 41,600 × 66% × 1.9 kg, plus flats 10,400 × 21% × 1.4 kg, × 52 weeks | **~2,870 t** |

A more realistic projection is about **2,870–2,930 tonnes**, roughly 11–13% below the study's figure. Pilots also tend to overstate long-term participation, because enthusiasm is highest at launch. A six-month pilot from January to June can't show whether participation lasts beyond that.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the tonnage

Section 4 says Brookfield can offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected projection of about 2,900 t leaves **about 1,100 tonnes a year** with nowhere to go at £38 a tonne. Neither the projection nor the savings take this into account. The surplus would have to go to:

- **the plant 46 miles away,** at an unknown gate fee, with much longer round trips. That means more fuel, more crew time, and possibly an extra vehicle or a transfer arrangement.
- **or incineration,** which saves nothing and defeats the purpose of the service.

So "treatment is local at a plant 14 miles away" is true for less than two-thirds of the food waste, and only until 2029. Brookfield's expansion would need confirming, too.

## 4. The service isn't shown to be fully funded

The cost lines in Table 2 are correct: £141,400 for vehicles (6 × £165,000 ÷ 7), £408,000 for crews (12 operatives × £34,000), £96,000 for fuel and maintenance and £88,000 for caddies, liners and communications, totalling £733,400. Collection costs depend on the number of households and rounds rather than on tonnage, so lower tonnage doesn't reduce them. It only reduces the savings.

Recalculated:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520k funding |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t, all to Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,400 | Covered (£29,600 spare) |
| Corrected tonnage (about 2,870 t), all to Brookfield | about £212,500 | about £520,900 | **Roughly break-even** |
| 1,800 t to Brookfield, the remaining ~1,070 t to the distant plant at the same fee, extra haulage ignored | about £212,500 | about £520,900 | Break-even at best |
| 1,800 t to Brookfield, the remainder saves nothing | £133,200 | **£600,200** | **About £80,000 short** |

Even in the most favourable corrected case, funding only just covers the net cost, before any extra haulage to the 46-mile plant. The study also leaves out several costs:

- **Cover for staff and vehicles.** The plan has six vehicles for six crews, with no spare for breakdowns or servicing, and no relief staff for leave and sickness. Covering 12 operatives typically adds 10–15% to staffing costs.
- **Supervision and management** of the new service.
- **Running the phone line and web page,** and handling caddy requests.
- **Any separate arrangements for flats,** following from point 1.
- **The upfront cash** for about £990,000 of vehicles and caddies for 52,000 households. Depreciation spreads the cost over time, but the Council still needs the capital or financing now, and financing costs aren't shown.

Finally, the funding is **provisional**. The Government has only "indicated" it. The study should say how certain it is, how long it will last, and what happens if it's lower.

## 5. Smaller points

- **The 81% satisfaction figure** comes from "surveyed pilot households." The study should give the sample size and response rate, because surveys like this often over-represent people who took part in the scheme.
- **The weighted average of 1.9 kg.** Strictly, the all-household figure is about 1.86 kg. Rounding it to 1.9 slightly overstates tonnage.
- **The timetable is tight.** Crews will be recruited only from February 2027 for an April start. HGV-licensed drivers can be hard to find, so recruitment should begin earlier. Delivering caddies to 52,000 homes within March is also a large logistics task. The Brookfield contract should be signed before the vehicle order is placed.
- **Contamination below 2% and falling missed collections** are genuinely good results and worth keeping.

## What holds up

- The pilot design: a real service, weekly measurement, and a split by housing type.
- The arithmetic in the cost table, and the £74-per-tonne saving.
- The vehicle lead time sensibly drives the timetable.
- Low contamination and positive feedback, subject to the survey caveat.

## Suggested changes before this goes to Cabinet

1. Report the flats result accurately and propose, with costs, a specific approach for flats.
2. Rebuild the tonnage projection from the pilot's housing-type rates (about 2,870 t), with a lower-participation scenario.
3. Plan for the roughly 1,100 t above Brookfield's capacity: name the destination, its gate fee and the extra haulage, and say what happens after 2029.
4. Add relief staff, a spare vehicle, supervision, the phone line and web page, and the flats approach to the costs. Show the upfront capital and how it will be financed.
5. Present the funding position as a range against the provisional allocation, and include a fallback if the allocation is lower.
6. Start crew recruitment earlier, and secure the Brookfield contract before ordering vehicles.

The roll-out may well be the right decision, and it may be a legal requirement anyway. But Cabinet should know that, on the pilot's own figures, the service is at best break-even against provisional funding and possibly about £80,000 a year short. It should also know that flats will need a different approach.
